paras: The burning of Henry Jenkins's house was a fire, believed to have been set, that destroyed the home of a Black carpenter just outside Newport News, Virginia, on the night of August 5, 1905. Jenkins, his wife and four children escaped, and he told the local paper that several people had threatened to burn the house.

Jenkins owned a one-story frame house situated just across the county line near Jefferson avenue and Nineteenth street, beyond the reach of the city's fire hoses. According to his own account, several people had made threats to burn his home before the fire; the report does not name them or say why they made the threats.

At about 11 o'clock that night, while the family slept, the house caught fire. Jenkins woke to the smoke and got his wife and children out before the building was engulfed. An alarm brought East End company No. 2 of the city fire department, but the firemen could not reach the building with the hose, and the house was completely destroyed.

Jenkins said he believed that one or all of the people who had threatened him carried out their threats, and he put the loss at $300, with no insurance. No report of an investigation or arrest appears in the coverage.

The Newport News Daily Press carried the only known report, a short page-one item on August 6 headlined "NEGRO HOME BURNED" with the deck "Henry Jenkins Believes His House Was Set Afire." The paper wrote that the fire was "believed to have been of incendiary origin" and attributed the threats to Jenkins, without comment on who might have set it or why. No coverage of the fire was found in other white papers or in the Black press.

reader.title: Burning of Henry Jenkins's house
bases: The only report describes a fire 'believed to have been of incendiary origin' that destroyed a Black carpenter's occupied home after unnamed people had threatened to burn it (A1).
A single Newport News Daily Press item reports the fire, and the arson claim rests on the paper's 'believed' and on Jenkins's own statement (A1).
